Fiji Rugby Launches Fijian Latui Programme, Names 37-Member Squad for European Assembly
article_text:
Fiji Rugby has officially launched the Fijian Latui Programme, marking a significant step towards strengthening player development pathways, expanding international opportunities and building Fiji’s presence in European rugby.

The programme was unveiled at Butt Street Hall in Suva today, alongside the announcement of a 37-member squad, comprising players from Fiji’s domestic competitions and overseas-based professional clubs.

Fiji Rugby Chief Executive Officer Koli Sewabu said the initiative represents more than establishing another Fijian rugby team in Europe. It is part of the organisation’s wider strategy to develop players, coaches and management personnel while creating opportunities that will ultimately benefit rugby in Fiji.

“For us, this is about much more than putting another Fijian rugby team on the field in Europe,” Sewabu said.

“It’s about giving our players and coaches more opportunities, building stronger relationships overseas and making sure Fiji Rugby is in a better position to benefit from the opportunities available in the international game.”

The Fijian Latui Programme forms part of Fiji Rugby’s commitment to Performance Excellence, with a focus on preparing emerging talent for the demands of professional and international rugby.

The squad brings together players competing in France, other overseas competitions and Fiji’s domestic rugby system, providing an opportunity for local talent to gain valuable exposure in a European rugby environment.

Of the 37 players named, 12 will travel from Fiji, including 10 representatives from the Skipper Cup competition, Fijian Drua prop Mesake Doge and New Zealand-based Samuela Tawake.

The Skipper Cup representatives include players from Naitasiri, Nadi, Nadroga, Suva, Ba and Kadavu, highlighting the continued importance of provincial rugby in developing Fiji’s next generation of international players.

Sewabu emphasised that the Latui Programme is designed to complement, rather than replace, Fiji’s existing domestic competitions and national development structures.

“The intention is to strengthen those existing pathways and, over time, give our national selectors a wider pool of players who are better prepared for international rugby,” he said.

The Fiji Rugby High-Performance Unit is working towards the squad’s planned assembly in France on 11 November 2026.

The programme will also provide professional development opportunities for Fijian coaches through direct exposure to European coaching systems and high-performance environments.

Former Flying Fijians Head Coach Patrice Lagisquet has been named Head Coach and Rugby Director of the Fijian Latui, supported by a coaching and management group comprising locally and internationally based personnel.

Three coaches travelling from Fiji, Senirusi Seruvakula, Kele Leawere and Cohen Politini, will work alongside Lagisquet and the Europe-based coaching staff as part of Fiji Rugby’s strategic coaching development initiatives.

The attachments are intended to strengthen coaching capabilities and contribute to improved performance across Fiji Rugby’s development and national programmes.

Sewabu said investing in coaching and management expertise is equally important to producing international-quality players.

“And that is important because we cannot focus only on developing players. We also need to develop the people who coach, manage and support them,” he said.

The Fiji Rugby Players Association (FRPA) has welcomed the launch, highlighting the importance of protecting players’ interests as they pursue professional opportunities overseas.

Speaking on behalf of the Association, Wame Lewaravu emphasised that the success of international player pathways must be measured not only through performances and contracts, but also through the wellbeing and long-term development of players.

“The proper channel is not a barrier. It is a safeguard,” the Association’s address stated.

The Association stressed the importance of ensuring that schools, provincial unions, Fiji Rugby and families remain involved in decisions concerning players moving into overseas professional rugby.

It also highlighted the challenges players can face when adapting to unfamiliar environments, including separation from family, cultural differences and the expectations that come with professional contracts.

“A player is first a person, a son or daughter, a member of a community. Their wellbeing, on and off the field, must be our first responsibility and never an afterthought.”

The Association reaffirmed its commitment to working with Fiji Rugby, schools, provincial unions and international partners to prepare players for overseas careers, strengthen welfare support and promote education and life beyond rugby.

Lewaravu has also been named in the Fijian Latui management structure in a player welfare role.

Beyond high-performance development, Fiji Rugby sees the Latui Programme as an opportunity to strengthen its relationships with international clubs, rugby organisations and commercial partners.

Sewabu said Fiji’s global rugby reputation provides a strong foundation for exploring new partnerships and revenue opportunities that can support the long-term sustainability of the game.

“We cannot continue to rely only on our traditional sources of funding. We need to explore new partnerships, new markets and new ways of generating revenue,” he said.

Fiji Rugby also acknowledged Axellerate Fiji for its offer of merchandise sponsorship support, which remains subject to the necessary commercial clearances.

Sewabu stressed that any commercial success generated through the programme must translate into meaningful investment in Fiji’s players, competitions and rugby development structures.

The launch of the Fijian Latui Programme represents another step in Fiji Rugby’s efforts to create a stronger connection between domestic development and the international professional game.

With 37 players selected and a coaching and management structure established, the programme aims to provide valuable experience, strengthen professional pathways and create opportunities for the next generation of Fijian rugby talent.

For Sewabu, the ultimate measure of the programme’s success will be its contribution to the future of rugby in Fiji.

“At the end of the day, our responsibility is to make Fiji Rugby stronger, not just for the players representing us today, but for those who will wear the white jersey in the years to come.”

title: Dan Lancaster reveals Scotland talks with Gregor Townsend
article_text:
Dan Lancaster has revealed that he held talks with Gregor Townsend before missing out on a call-up to the Scotland squad for the Nations Championship.

Last week, Townsend announced his group for the upcoming games against New Zealand, Australia and Japan at Murrayfield, plus finals weekend at Twickenham.

Finn Russell is Scotland’s undisputed starter at fly-half as one of the best number 10s in rugby, while Fergus Burke, Tom Jordan and Blair Kinghorn provide back-up.

Scotland have good depth in the position with Adam Hastings not selected and Jake Dalziel viewed as the heir to Russell’s throne.

Realistically, Lancaster is currently an outside shout for a call-up but he’s been good for Glasgow this campaign after stepping up to be their leading fly-half.

The 25-year-old started five of six games in the first block of fixtures with Glasgow unbeaten and he had a zoom call with Townsend ahead of the squad announcement.

Asked whether he had any contact with Townsend, Lancaster replied: “Yes, I had a Zoom call and a voice note. They went with the three. Again, that's not in my control.

“There are pros and cons. Obviously, you want to be in that situation. The pro for me is that I get a couple of weeks off to reset my body, reset physically and mentally, and have a bit of downtime.

“So there are pros and cons. You want to be in that situation, but it is what it is. I'm sure he speaks to everyone who's Scottish-qualified.”

Franco Smith has afforded his non-international players some time off during the break and Lancaster is heading to Miami - with dad Stuart - for some winter sun.

Warriors head coach Smith goes to great pains to dispute that Lancaster isn’t the ‘main-man’ at fly-half for Glasgow.

That fact, however, is irrefutable and the former Racing 92 man is happy with his form so far this season.

“Obviously, I'm happy to get a run of games. There are good tens behind me as well. There's a great group of tens. Charlie (Savala) is still to come back. Matthew Urwin did an unbelievable job when he played and Bayley (Kuenzle) can play there.

“I'm happy to get time in the saddle. I feel like I'm seeing space pretty well, there’s stuff to work on but overall. I’m happy.

“I think we've grown as an attack. As a result, we're averaging five tries at home. And there's still so much of our attack we can be better at. I think probably the best we've played over an 80-minute period was that Sale game. That's probably the most it's looked like for us.

“So I'm glad that we're scoring a lot of points. There's still so much we can do better as well. Because we've got that experience outside me, it just makes my job easier. I can really focus on my game."

Korea Open: Wang to Remember
article_text:
It was a match to remember in Yeosu as Wang Yu-kai produced the biggest upset of the opening round at the YEOSU VICTOR Korea Open 2026, toppling top seed and compatriot Chou Tien Chen 21-18 16-21 21-12 to reach the last 16.

The win marked a milestone for the youngster, who had lost both of his previous meetings with Chou in straight games.

“I think you could consider it an achievement. Before the match, my goal was to push my senior to three games,” Wang shared.

“In our previous two encounters, I lost 0-2 both times, so this time I wanted to take the match to a deciding third game and really give him a fight.”

The victory was made all the more significant by Wang’s long-standing admiration for Chou, whose matches he studied while coming through the ranks.

“Yes. I used to learn a lot by watching my senior’s match videos, and I’ve also had the opportunity to train with him before. I know that he’s a very determined and dedicated player, so there are many aspects of his game and attitude that I look up to and try to learn from.”

Wang admitted the match was far from straightforward, particularly when momentum began to shift.

“First of all, this match has given me a lot more confidence for future competitions, and I’ve also learned a great deal from my senior. I’ve gained a better understanding of how to approach similar situations in the future, how to respond to each rally, and how to handle different shots.

“During the match, I still found myself rushing things a little, especially when he started catching up in the score. I became quite nervous at those moments. But after playing this match, I have a better idea of how to adjust and deal with these situations next time.”

The win comfortably surpassed the target Wang had set for himself at the start of the week.

“My original goal was simply to win at least one match in the main draw. This was my first Super 500 tournament. Previously, when I made it through the qualifying rounds and reached the main draw, I was eliminated in the round of 32. So this result means a lot to me and has given me a huge confidence boost.”

Next up is another familiar face, with Wang set to face compatriot Wang Tzu Wei in the second round.

“I might watch some of his match videos again. I hope I can perform at my best, stay relaxed, and avoid getting too nervous when facing my senior.”

Yoo Tae Bin gave the home fans plenty to cheer on Day defeating world No.38 Prannoy H.S. 23-21 21-15 and book his place in the second round.

Playing in front of a partisan crowd in Yeosu, Yoo showed maturity beyond his years to overcome H.S, edging a tense opening game before pulling away in the second. The Korean shuttler remained patient throughout, refusing to be drawn into forcing the issue against one of the tour’s giant hitters.

“Since my opponent is a relatively experienced player, I felt it was important to engage in longer rallies and be patient in my approach. He has a great deal of experience, so I also tried not to rush things at any point.”

The result was another encouraging step in what has already been a breakthrough season for Yoo, highlighted by his Asian Games bronze medal. He admitted there was extra motivation whenever he competed on home soil.

“First of all, tournaments held in Korea have always meant a lot to me, and they naturally make me want to be even more focused and give my best. For a tournament like the Korea Open, I really wanted to achieve a good result, so I think I put extra effort into preparing thoroughly beforehand.”

Yoo’s measured style and movement around the court have drawn comparisons with some of the sport’s leading names, but the Korean revealed that the player he has learned the most from is Olympic champion Chen Long.

“I’ve learned a lot from Chen. I’ve watched quite a few of his match videos and picked up many things from him. In that sense, Chen Long is a role model for me.”

He will take on Yudai Okimoto with a quarterfinals spot at stake.

title: Lucas Herbert Reveals Major Reason For LIV Golf Exit
article_text:
Lucas Herbert says a lack of both quantity and quality events on the proposed LIV Golf 2.0 was a big reason behind him turning his back on the team tour and heading back to the DP World Tour.

On top of that, though, his desire to get into and shine in the Majors more often prompted his decision to join the ranks of players ruling out signing up for LIV Golf 2.0.

Herbert finished fourth on the LIV Golf standings after two wins last season, but still decided that his future lies away from the team-based tour and away from the all-Australian Ripper GC.

Herbert equalling the Major record with a round of 62 at the Open Championship this year showed him how close he could get to winning a Major - and now he wants more of that feeling.

And from what he's heard from LIV insiders, Herbert doesn't feel there's enough for him to achieve his goals if he remains.

“From what it sounds like, it’ll be 10 tournaments. They’re telling us that there’s going to be potentially more events to play outside of those as extra playing opportunities,” Herbert told the Tee It Up podcast.

“I’m unsure how they’re going to make that work. I’m unsure what kind of fields those are going to be.

“10 events is not enough to build a season around. You could maybe sneak a couple more in there, but the more you play, the sort of lower quality they are. It’s quality over quantity."

Herbert was cited as a creditor for over $1m in the LIV bankruptcy filings, but he insists he's not aware of money matters as only Major access interests him right now.

title: Patrick Reed happy to be chasing Race to Dubai glory in the desert - Articles - Rolex Series
article_text:
Patrick Reed returns to the desert this week confident he can rediscover his early season form and become just the second American to be crowned Europe's Number One.

The 2018 Masters winner enjoyed a stunning International Swing in the Middle East in January and February, winning a maiden Rolex Series title at the Dubai Desert Classic, losing in a play-off at the Bapco Energies Bahrain Championship and then winning the Qatar Masters in consecutive weeks.

That catapulted him to the top of the Race to Dubai Rankings Delivered by DP World and there he sat for most of the season until Eugenio Chacarra's third victory of the campaign at last month's DP World India Championship saw the Spaniard replace him.

He now arrives back in the region for the DP World Tour Play-Offs, with enhanced points on offer at this week's Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship and the season-ending DP World Tour Championship.

Having already claimed 2,259.70 of his 3,474.62 Race to Dubai points in the desert this year, he rightly arrives at Yas Links full of confidence and ready to do battle in his attempt to fulfil a lifelong ambition.

"It's always been a goal of mine to win the Race to Dubai and hopefully we can knock that off this year," he said.

"I feel great. Obviously we've played in the desert really well this year. Kind of feel like the game is trending in a spot that I really need it to be right now.

"So yeah, we feel good and comfortable but obviously these two weeks are very important with not only just the Race but with the elevated points, going out there and trying to hopefully hoist up another trophy."

Having spent most of the season as the man to catch, Reed is now having to chase, with any of him, Chacarra, Rory McIlroy and Casey Jarvis able to top the Rankings come Sunday.

The 36-year-old is not looking to change his approach, however, and is keeping his focus on trying to win tournaments.

"It's always fun leading, that's for sure," he said. "It's always fun being out in front. But we are in a good position, sitting there in second and being able to chase and hunt him down.

"But a lot can happen in two weeks. Obviously later in the weeks is when you start thinking of, 'hey, do I need to press or not'. But I've always looked at every week trying to go out and compete and have chance to win at that time and that week. So really, the game plan still stays the same

"You can get yourself in a lot of trouble thinking too far ahead and being too aggressive, and what got me to this position is playing my game and my type of golf. That's how I feel comfortable and that's how I'm going to attack going in there."

Reed will be paired with Chacarra and McIlroy in round one, renewing a rivalry with the Northern Irishman that has provided plenty of entertainment down the years.

Their singles match at the 2016 Ryder Cup and battle down the stretch at the 2023 Hero Dubai Desert Classic will continue to live long in the memory and Reed is happy to be once again playing with his old adversary.

"I always love playing against Rory," he said. "I always pride myself on wanting to go out against the best and play against the best but obviously with his record and kind of what he's done throughout his career, he's one of the best golfers to play the game.

"So to be able to go out there and go nose-to-nose with him and play against him is something I always cherish and really enjoy doing. It should be fun."

title: Cardiff sign Welsh lock Green from Harlequins
article_text:
Cardiff have signed former Wales Under-20s lock Jonny Green from Harlequins with immediate effect.

The 22-year-old arrives on what the Blue and Blacks call a "long-term deal" and will aim to make his debut after the November break for the Nations Championship.

Green, who played 30 times for Quins and signed a contract extension last December, joins after the announcement that George Nott will retire in December.

"He's a big, physical lock, standing over 6ft 7ins, and there's a nice weight to him, but the biggest thing is his rugby pedigree and his motivation," said Cardiff head coach Corniel van Zyl.

"As with any young second-row there is stuff to work on, but he has a huge appetite to improve."

Green was born in Sussex and qualifies for Wales through his mother's side of the family, with his parents now living in Gowerton.

He played for Wales in two World Rugby U20 Championships and was invited to train with the senior national squad during the 2024 Six Nations.

The lock is ready to battle with Teddy Williams, Josh McNally, Rory Thornton and Tom Manz for game time at Cardiff.

Green said: "The main things I bring are physicality and work rate, they are the two foundations I always review my performances against, so hopefully I can bring that to Cardiff.

"I am very grateful to Harlequins for the opportunities they have given me and I have loved my time there, but I'm now looking forward to the next chapter in my career and kicking on at Cardiff."

The Blue and Blacks are seventh in the United Rugby Championship (URC) and are next in action against Ulster at the Arms Park on Saturday, 5 December (15:00 GMT).

11 Nations to Converge in Kenya for 2026 Rugby Africa Women’s Sevens Championship
article_text:
Kenya is set to host 11 nations for the 2026 Rugby Africa Women’s Sevens Championship scheduled for November 7 and 8 at the RFUEA Grounds in Nairobi, placing the HSBC SVNS 3 competition up for grabs.

In a statement on Wednesday, November 4, Sports Cabinet Secretary Salim Mvurya said the competition would feature teams from across the continent, with South Africa, Uganda and Madagascar among the participating sides.

Join our WhatsApp Channel for the latest news updates.

"The tournament will bring together 11 teams to compete for the African title, with a place in the HSBC SVNS 3 also at stake. Joining hosts Kenya are Burkina Faso, Ghana, Madagascar, Mauritius, Rwanda, South Africa, Tunisia, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe," the statement read.

Mvurya said hosting the continental competition formed part of its broader ambition to position Kenya as a major destination for international sporting events while creating more opportunities for women athletes.

"Hosting the championship advances Kenya’s commitment to becoming a leading destination for major sporting events. It also provides a platform to grow women’s rugby and showcase the talent emerging across the continent," the statement added.

Mvurya also welcomed the participating teams and their supporters, saying the tournament would offer visitors an opportunity to experience Kenya beyond the sporting competition.

"On behalf of the Government of Kenya, I welcome all participating teams and their supporters to Nairobi and invite our visitors to experience Kenya’s exceptional hospitality beyond the rugby field," the statement further read.

According to Mvurya, the Kenya Lionesses entered the competition following an impressive performance at the Safari Sevens, where they defeated Uganda 22-5 in the final to successfully defend their title.

With the tournament expected to attract significant attention from rugby fans, the Ministry urged Kenyans to attend the matches and support the national team.

"I urge Kenyans to turn out in large numbers at the RFUEA Grounds and give our Lionesses the backing they deserve. Tickets are already available through Tikohub.com," the statement noted.

The championship also came as Kenyan rugby celebrated a historic achievement at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, where the Rising Lionesses secured gold after defeating Australia 17-12 in an extra-time final.

The young Kenyan side had demonstrated impressive form throughout the competition, beginning with a 12–5 victory over China before recording a commanding 19–0 win against hosts Senegal.

They subsequently defeated Madagascar 15-5 in the semi-final to book their place in the final, where they overcame Australia to claim the gold medal.

Mvurya said the achievement marked a historic first for the continent, with Kenya becoming the first African nation to win rugby sevens gold at either the Olympic Games or the Youth Olympic Games.

"Their victory made Kenya the first African nation to win rugby sevens gold at either the Olympic Games or the Youth Olympic Games. I congratulate the players, coaches, technical bench and support staff. Their hard work throughout the campaign and their composure in a closely contested final have made Kenya proud," the statement concluded.

Elsewhere, Kenya has qualified 53 athletes across 13 sporting disciplines for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal.

In a statement on Sunday, November 1, the Ministry of Sports said Kenya had joined the global sporting fraternity in celebrating the start of the Games, describing the event as a defining moment for African sport.

The Kenyan contingent will feature athletes competing in athletics, rugby sevens, basketball 3x3, swimming, boxing, cycling, fencing, judo, Baseball5, beach handball, beach wrestling, triathlon and wushu.

Of the 53 athletes, 41 are female, representing 77 per cent of the country's qualified contingent and highlighting the strong representation of young women in Kenya's sporting programme.

The Ministry described the team's participation as an important opportunity for emerging athletes to compete internationally and showcase their abilities.

"Team Kenya’s participation in this landmark sporting event is a moment of immense national pride, providing an exceptional platform for our young athletes to showcase their talent, compete against the world’s best and contribute to a new chapter in Africa’s sporting history," the statement read.

The government said Kenya's presence at the Games was part of a broader strategy to strengthen the country's talent development system and prepare promising athletes for senior international competitions.

"Our presence in Dakar is anchored on a deliberate and long-term vision to strengthen Kenya’s sporting talent development pipeline.

"The Youth Olympic Games provide a critical transition platform through which promising young athletes gain exposure to elite international competition, develop the resilience and discipline required at the highest levels and prepare for progression into senior national teams," the statement added.

The Ministry urged the athletes to uphold the country's sporting values and use the international competition as an opportunity to inspire other young people interested in pursuing sports careers.

"To Team Kenya, this is your moment to demonstrate the discipline, resilience, determination and excellence that define our nation's sporting heritage. You represent a new generation entrusted with carrying forward Kenya’s proud Olympic tradition while establishing your own legacy on the international stage.

"Compete with integrity, uphold the highest standards of sportsmanship and embrace this opportunity to learn, grow and inspire millions of young Kenyans who aspire to follow in their footsteps," the statement concluded.

title: Scrum mechanics and a Gatland cameo: behind the scenes with the Nations Championship’s 13th team
article_text:
The 13th team participating at the Nations Championship this month are an intriguing bunch. If you didn’t know much about rugby and had wandered into a first-floor conference room at a hotel near Windsor on Monday you might almost have mistaken them for a gathering of airline pilots from nearby Heathrow. Slim, intelligent, studious … you’d trust them to stay calm on the flight deck.

Stick them in matchday kit, however, and the world’s top rugby union referees do not always enjoy universal respect, certainly online. They can be unflappably brilliant for 79 and a half minutes and yet still be defined by one hairline call barely visible to the naked eye. Every Test in which they are involved is an away game and, popularity wise, they often receive the same unconditional love as traffic wardens and the chancellor of the exchequer.

A few hours in the company of, among others, Karl Dickson, Luke Pearce, Angus Gardner, Ben O’Keefe and Hollie Davidson is to get a rare glimpse of the flip side. And to wonder why World Rugby has previously not made a bigger deal of the pre-match lengths to which today’s referees now go. Try doing the equivalent of a geometry exam while simultaneously having to run at least nine kilometres, explain your pivotal decisions to millions on TV and ignore the collective screech of 80,000 agitated spectators. Tough doesn’t remotely cover it.

Particularly when rugby’s lawbook is so notoriously labyrinthine. One of the keynote sessions we attend, for example, concerns the internal mechanics of the scrum. The former Wales captain Jonathan Humphreys, now World Rugby’s scrum consultant, explains the vital importance of ensuring loosehead props do not have their inside shoulders tucked before engagement, thus crucially skewing the whole angle of their front row and, all too often, the opposition’s as well. Video clips are duly shown to illustrate the potential ramifications.

Cue a cameo appearance from the former British & Irish Lions head coach Warren Gatland, a World Rugby coaching consultant these days, who comes up from the back of the room to bind on to Humphreys and demonstrate the precise shoulders-back, pre-engage position that officials should be mandating. Talk about poachers turned gamekeepers.

Then there is the hooker’s “brake foot”, so called because of its importance in stabilising the scrum. If the heel of the hooker’s front foot is not flat to the ground, a free-kick should be awarded. Got that? No heads on shoulders before engagement – front-rowers should instead be aligned temple to temple – make sure everyone pushes straight rather than walking around, no guesswork, etc etc. Forty minutes have passed and no one has even mentioned that backs play rugby, too.

All joking aside, it does seem the sport is inching slightly closer to the holy grail: a consistent balance between attack and defence, more clear-cut messaging and a product that satisfies players of both sexes and spectators of all ages. World Rugby even has a fresh four-pillar mantra when it comes to enhancing the game: protect the player, embrace the contest, promote continuity, win the fan. Tick all four boxes and, hopefully, greater interest and investment will follow.

And the penny also seems to be dropping globally that referees need to be backed to make their own strong decisions, for better or worse, rather than the game being fractured endlessly by unnecessary television match official interventions.

In the end perfection matters less than big calls around tries and dangerous play being managed correctly. “Get what matters. The rest doesn’t matter,” one leading official urges, stressing the “clear and obvious” ethos which forms the basis of modern whistleblowing.

Equally, though, teams may have to brace themselves for a few extra free-kicks and penalties early in games over the coming month as referees and players alike get up to speed with the latest sanctions for hip and knee drop tackles as well as the updated head-contact process around the breakdown, designed to reduce dangerous flying clear-outs among other things. The reality is that players’ habits will change only when they are effectively given no other option.

There was also a significant initiative on Sunday when virtually all the world’s leading head coaches met the top referees to exchange their hopes and fears for the game’s future. The smart money is on certain aspects looking appreciably different.

Among the concepts being lobbed around, for example, are special refereeing goggles capable of showing the aerial view of a scrum, thus making awkward culpability calls slightly easier. Another suggestion is a separate specialist scrum referee – David Flatman, come on down – who would be invited to, er, sprint on and adjudicate on set pieces.

More research, incidentally, is also being commissioned to identify the parts of the game that fans most enjoy, assisted by the use of heart rate monitors. Early southern hemisphere studies have shown that heart rates soar for interceptions, line breaks and the haka, with the biggest turn-offs being dull interruptions and scrum resets.

Recent stats also show the ratio of tries scored compared to penalty goals in major Tests has trebled in less than three years. Once the 2027 World Cup is over the debate surrounding the shape of the game seems certain to reignite.

In the meantime, here’s to the seriously dedicated men and women at the sharp end. Next time you’re tempted to shout ‘You don’t know what you’re doing’ from your vantage point 100 metres away, be assured they absolutely do. And also bear in mind the most timeless rugby mantra of the lot: no referee, no game.

title: Warren Gatland and ex-Wales coach land new consultancy roles as summit held
article_text:
Former Wales coaches Warren Gatland and Jonathan Humphreys have both landed new consultancy jobs with World Rugby.

Gatland left his second stint with Wales midway through the 2025 Six Nations, following a 14-Test losing run. Humphreys, who worked as Wales' forward coach under Wayne Pivac and Gatland, then departed ahead of last year's summer tour of Japan.

Gatland has held the odd consultancy role, turning down a director of rugby role at Harlequins earlier this year.

He was also understood to have applied to become Fiji's head coach - although he has since denied that.

The pair are now working with World Rugby.

Humphreys is World Rugby's scrum consultant, while Gatland is a World Rugby coaching consultant.

Both were present this week as World Rugby's referees and officials got together for a conference - with Humphreys leading a presentation on scrums.

A special focus will be put on certain aspects of the scrum this month in the Nations Championship, as explained by Humphreys.

Both loosehead props will need to have their right shoulders out ahead of the engagement, while the hooker must have his brake foot grounded in the tunnel to ensure the scrum stays stable.

The previous day, the top 24 international head coaches had met with World Rugby officials to discuss the future of the game.

Earlier this year, Humphreys had spoken to WalesOnline about leaving his coaching role with Wales - saying he was taking a break from the game.

“I'm not bitter about leaving because if you lose 17 games in a row you're lucky to stay in a job," he said. "So I have no issue that they wanted to go a different way.

“I loved my time with Wales and I was proud to win the Six Nations and beat the Springboks for the first time out in South Africa, but everything must come to an end at some point.

“I will always look back at my time in the job with an equal measure of pride and disappointment.

“I have taken a big break because I haven’t had one for 35 years.

“I have taken a complete break which I have very much enjoyed. I have loved it. I haven’t missed rugby at all.

“With Wales, towards the end, you knew it was going to be a massive struggle to compete. All that comes with the stresses of it all.

“Until you have actually taken yourself away from it, you don’t know how much effect that has on you.

“It’s again like having the Welsh captaincy taken off me. It’s like a relief and I feel a lot better for it.

“I’m more relaxed and your emotions are not up and down on a weekly basis.”
